Electromagnetism. The unified theory of electricity and magnetism, formalized by James Clerk Maxwell in the eighteen sixties. It reveals that electric and magnetic fields are two aspects of a single phenomenon, and that accelerating charges produce waves that propagate at the speed of light. This framework underpins all of classical physics and revealed that light itself is an electromagnetic wave.

The foundation rests on several key principles. Gauss's law states that charges create electric fields, and the total flux through a surface equals the enclosed charge divided by permittivity. Faraday's law shows that changing magnetic flux induces an electric field, which is the basis of electric generators and transformers. The Ampère-Maxwell law demonstrates that currents and changing electric fields produce magnetic fields.

Maxwell unified these four equations into a coherent framework predicting electromagnetic waves traveling at the speed of light. The electric field from a positive charge points away from the charge. The field from a negative charge points inward. In an electromagnetic wave, perpendicular electric and magnetic fields oscillate in phase, with both perpendicular to the direction of propagation.

The magnetic field is one component of the unified field. The electric field is the other component and is inseparable from magnetism. Photons are electromagnetic waves quantized as light particles. Electromagnetic waves are the wave phenomenon predicted by Maxwell's equations. Magnetic force is the force on moving charges in magnetic fields. And James Clerk Maxwell formulated the unifying equations.
